title: A Ballet of Lepers
author: Leonard Cohen
description: I wasn’t really sure what to expect of Cohen’s early ventures into writing as a big fan of his music, but I would not consider this a high point of his oeuvre. His typical lecherous style doesn’t land here as well as it does in a song, where plots can run loose; here, the title short story suffers from over-musing and doesn’t develop much. The play, too, was plain odd. I found a few of the short stories to be the most palatable. “Polly” in particular might make it into some anthology, but most everything else was a worthy sacrifice for Cohen’s musical career.

title: Native Son
author: Richard Wright
description: So difficult in the best way. Richard Wright is a fantastic writer who flawlessly conveys the heft of Bigger’s story.

title: Regeneration
author: Pat Barker
description: I found this a bit... lackluster? Perhaps it’s because I am so disconnected geographically and temporally from Barker’s original audience, but there wasn’t much of a plot to latch onto. Many of the chapters cycle through the same general format (one of the patients does something, then back to Rivers), which did not make for strong engagement as the novel progressed. It mostly felt like filler in a true story that didn’t need to become a novel.

title: Dune
author: Frank Herbert
description: I don’t often read science fiction, but what a treat it was. I really understood while reading the book more so than watching the movie how this became the blueprint for all science fiction literature that followed. In my opinion, it dragged a bit in the third act, but not so terribly as to mar my impression of Herbert and the series.

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
description:
“‘The right to grow old and ugly and impotent; the right to have syphilis and cancer; the right to have too little to eat; the right to be lousy; the right to live in constant apprehension of what may happen tomorrow; the right to catch typhoid; the right to be tortured by unspeakable pains of every kind.’ There was a long silence.
‘I claim them all,’ said the Savage at last.”
A lovely read. I wish there’d been a slightly stronger arc for Lenina and Bernard but I understand why there wasn’t. Definitely interesting to read with my knowledge of the USSR.

title: The Beautiful and Damned
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
description: It took me genuinely two years to read this because I couldn’t get past the first part the first two times I tried. Anthony Patch is such a bore, and even if you’re supposed to feel some loathsome sympathy over his degenerate loaferism, you remember that he’s a reflection of the author and question how much larger than life his insufferability is. Gloria saves the second act by having at least *something* going for her, but Anthony’s undeserved auspice concludes the novel with straight frustration.

title: Martyr!
author: Kaveh Akbar
description: It feels like it’s been a long time since I’ve read a truly enjoyable book, and I think that shows in that I tore through this in a few days when books normally take me months. It makes up for any of its imperfections in wholehearted discovery. Because I have the awareness of a pillbug while reading, the twist floored me, but even if I had recognized it ahead of time, I would applaud Akbar’s accretion toward a third-act triumph.

title: Unfree Labor: American Slavery and Russian Serfdom
author: Peter Kolchin
description: My first foray into comparitive history. Though I found some of the distinctions between serfdom and slavery overreaching and others self-evident, I think my criticisms had more to do with the nature of the content than Kolchin’s research. An altogether interesting accompaniment to my study of Russian history.

title: The Paris Review Interviews, vol. 1
description: I mean, I’m unlikely to speak negatively of anything involving Joan Didion. It was so worthwhile to read the insights of these luminaries, some my idols, some new to me, all brilliant in their own voices. It’s funny to read the interviews of these people and know exactly how they think, and even funnier to know how insufferable some of them must have been (looking at you, Truman Capote). Some of these interviewees—Borges, Billy Wilder, Didion of course—only grew in my perception after reading this. I’m lucky to have had this gifted to me.

title: My Brilliant Friend
author: Elena Ferrante
description: I was quite excited for this book. I wouldn’t say it met the high praise it recieves—I found the plot just as ambling as its pleonastic sentences. It’s still a personal and touching read, but I should’ve known better than to pick a book with a review from Gwyneth Paltrow quoted on the cover.

title: The Best American Short Stories 2025
description: While some of the stories in this edition were wholly worth the “best” moniker, others lead me to doubt Ng’s curatorial abilities. My favorites were “Seven Stories About Tammy” by Elizabeth McCracken—an engrossing multiperspective anthology packed into a concise format—and “Gray, Cotton, White Lace Edges” by Isabelle Fang—a reflective, shocking feat. Others filled out the collection well: “Aishwarya Rai” by Sanjana Thakur and “Third Room” by Julian Robles were both perfectly enjoyable reads. But others lagged noticeably behind. I found the writing in “Maritza and Carmen” by Lyn di Iorio in dire need of an edit, and I didn’t even finish the whole 15 pages of “Time of the Preacher” by Bret Anthony Johnston. I found the editor’s inclusion of several stories referencing, directly or indirectly, the COVID-19 pandemic bizarrely out-of-touch. At its heart, this seems to be a poorly constructed collection, despite its standout talents.

title: The Woman Destroyed
author: Simone de Beauvoir
description: A collection of three medium-length stories, all centered on women and their unhappy marriages. My favorite was the second, "The Monologue," which is written as the rant of a woman separated from her husband and bereaved of her daughter. It’s a poignant, inventive stream of consciousness, sometimes a bit hard to follow but nevertheless satisfactory. The place where I truly struggled was with the titular novella, which follows a woman obsessively clinging to her adulterous husband and going insane over the affair. Perhaps it’s my modernist skew which de Beauvoir targets, but this was quite a frustrating read, to watch idly as Monique wastes away mere steps from the exit to her misery and her marriage. I also took issue with this translation; any copyeditor worth their salt should have caught the use of “vexed” every five pages (yes, I counted.)

title: Dreyer’s English: An Utterly Correct Guide to Clarity and Style
author: Benjamin Dreyer
description: A clever and satisfying glimpse into the world of copyediting where I spend far too much time. A reference book that reads like fiction, yet simultaneously one I want to keep on hand. I found chapters 2 and 7 particularly edifying and entertaining.
